# How to Save Your Preferences So Every New AI Chat Starts Closer to What You Want

> **In short:** You can write a short, reusable note describing your audience, tone and format, then save it in your assistant's standing-instructions setting or paste it at the start of each new chat. The main thing to know: the assistant only follows what it can see, and saved-settings features vary by app and plan.

By the end of this guide, you will have a short note that explains who you are, who your answers are for, and how you like information presented. You will also know where to keep that note so you stop re-explaining yourself every time you open a new chat. This is for people who already use an AI chat tool for everyday tasks and are tired of starting from zero.

## Before you start
- An account with an AI chat assistant you already use, and a way to open it on your phone or computer.
- A notes app or any plain text document, so you can draft your note somewhere safe.
- Time: about 20 minutes, most of it spent on the draft. Some saved-settings features depend on your app version or plan, so check what yours offers as you go.

## Step 1 — Decide what your note should cover
Before you write anything, list three things: who you are (your job, school or hobby), who your answers are usually for (yourself, customers, students, your team), and how you like answers shaped (short or detailed, bullets or paragraphs, friendly or formal). Open your notes app and jot down one line for each. You do not need perfect wording yet. What you should see is a short list of plain facts about you.

If you are not sure how to phrase it, ask the assistant to help you draft it. Start a new chat and type the example below, filling in your own details. The assistant should respond with a short draft you can edit. It usually takes a few seconds. If the draft is too long or too stiff, reply with "shorter, please" and it will usually trim it.

💬 Example: "Help me write a short note about my preferences for an AI assistant. I am a [job title], I write mostly for [your audience], and I like answers that are [tone] and organized as [format]."

You'll know it worked when you have a rough list of three to five sentences describing you and how you want answers.

## Step 2 — Write the reusable block
Now turn your list into one compact block of text, roughly 60 to 120 words, that the assistant can read in seconds. Use plain sentences in the first person, for example: who you are, who the answers are for, the tone you want, the format you want, and anything to avoid. Keep it under about 150 words, because very long notes tend to be skimmed or only partly followed. Save this block in your notes app under a clear title, such as "AI preferences," so you can find it again.

The block is the part you will copy later, so it is worth reading it aloud once. If a sentence sounds like a rule you would not actually follow, cut it. Remove any private details you would not want stored, such as account numbers, addresses or health information.

💬 Example: "I am a [job title] at a small [industry] company. My answers are for [your audience], so keep the tone friendly and plain. Use short bullet points, put the main point first, and avoid jargon unless you explain it."

You'll know it worked when your block reads clearly to someone who has never met you, and it fits on one phone screen without scrolling much.

## Step 3 — Save it where the assistant keeps standing instructions
Open your assistant's settings and look for something like custom instructions, personalization, or a memory or saved-information section. Some apps also let you create a project or folder and attach standing notes to it, so every chat inside that project starts with your note. The names and locations vary, so if you do not see these exact words, search the settings for "instructions," "personalize" or "memory." Paste your block into the box, then save.

Once saved, the assistant may read the note in future chats automatically. Not every app works this way, and some features may be limited depending on your plan, so check the help text in the settings area. If you cannot find any saved-instructions option at all, skip to Step 4 and paste the block by hand each time.

You'll know it worked when the settings page shows your note as saved, and the app confirms the change without an error message.

## Step 4 — Test it in a brand-new chat
Start a completely new chat, so nothing from earlier conversations sits above your question. Then ask something you normally ask, such as a summary, a plan or an explanation. Watch the answer: does the length, tone and format match your note? If you saved your block in settings, you should not need to paste anything. If you did not, paste your block at the top of the message, then type your question underneath.

If the answer ignores your note, check that the saved setting is switched on, then try again. If the answer follows your note only partly, that is common. Ask a follow-up such as "Please make this shorter and use bullet points," and note what it changed. Those corrections tell you which part of your block needs more precise wording.

💬 Example: "Summarize the main steps for [task you do often] in [number] short bullet points."

You'll know it worked when the answer is noticeably closer to your preferred length and style, without you having to correct it first.

## Step 5 — Refine the note after a few real chats
After you have used the note for a week or two, review it once. Ask yourself whether any sentence is unclear, out of date or unnecessary. Maybe your audience changed, or you now want shorter answers. Edit only the sentence that caused the problem, then save again. Keep the total length close to where it was, because a crowded note can dilute the parts that matter most.

To check the edit, start one new chat and repeat a question you tested before. Compare the two answers side by side. If the new one is clearly better, keep it. If it is worse, go back to your previous version, which you should have kept in your notes app.

💬 Example: "Please rewrite my preferences note so it is under [number] words and keeps the same tone."

You'll know it worked when your note is shorter or clearer, and the answers you get match what you actually want more often.

## Common mistakes
- **Writing a huge note.** A long list of rules is easy to write and hard to follow. Keep the block to a short paragraph or a few sentences, and cut anything that does not change the answers you get.
- **Expecting perfect memory.** Saved instructions guide the assistant, but they do not guarantee every answer will match. Always skim the answer, and ask for a correction if something is off. Your note improves results; it does not replace your review.
- **Saving private details.** It is tempting to include your full address, passwords or health details so the assistant "knows everything." The fix is simple: keep the note to your work style and preferences, and leave out anything sensitive you would not want stored.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A note saying you want short, friendly answers can make recipes, travel plans or homework help feel more relevant from the first message.
- **For your business or work:** A note describing your team, your customers and the format you want for reports can save you from repeating the same setup every time you draft an email or summary.
- **If you want to go further:** Try keeping two or three notes for different jobs, such as one for writing and one for planning, and attach each to a separate project or chat. Just remember that the assistant still needs your review, and that some saved-settings features may depend on your plan.

## Try it now
Open your notes app and write three plain sentences: who you are, who your answers are for, and one format you prefer. Then start a new chat, paste those sentences above a question you ask every week, and compare the answer with what you usually get. You will know right away whether the note is pointing in the right direction.
